core <- od |> filter(is_core_aligned)

# Consistent publication theme for both HTML and PDF
theme_rail <- function(base_size = 10) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +

      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#0f172a", size = base_size + 1.5),

}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Purpose and audience.** This technical note is written for the project's consultancy economists and Dr John Nellthorp (ITS, University of Leeds). It audits the active travel demand modelling completed to date across `railactive`, sets out a transparent, first-principles uptake methodology explicitly aligned with Active Travel England's *Active Mode Benefits: Theoretical Framework* [@nellthorp2026], illustrates the method on the **`r tot_len_km` km Oxfordshire-to-Uxbridge** corridor using 2011 Census OD commuting data, specifies the exact output datasets for DfT AMAT / TAG / TATE3030 economic appraisal, and lists the strategic modelling choices to agree before scaling to the full North–South Greenway.
:::

---

## Assessment of Existing RailActive Uptake Work {#sec-assessment}

Before designing the full-corridor economic appraisal pipeline, we audited the analytical work completed across the three `railactive` repositories (`railactive/pipeline`, `railactive/hs2cycle`, `railactive/amat`) and the interactive `/netassign` viewer.

### What Has Been Delivered and Verified

1. **Harmonised corridor alignment (`north_south_corridor_v2.json`, v0.5.2):** An 805.6 km preferred North–South Greenway spine (385.7 km core HS2 alignment plus southern Avenue Verte and northern Stoke–Birkenhead branches) classified into a 3-tier status taxonomy (`preferred`, `alternative`, `superseded`) and explicit HS2 civil-asset designations (`Repurposed HS2 TCR`, `HS2 delivered greenway`, `Dual Use MATs`).
2. **Multi-purpose network assignment and counter validation (`pipeline` Phases 1–4):** Using the Rust/CSIS `netassign` engine, the preferred greenway was topologically spliced into a 1.72-million-link corridor network (`Scenario A` baseline vs `Scenario B` High-LoS Greenway, with DEM gradients capped at $\pm 2\%$ on engineered alignments) and validated against **7,219 cycling** and **1,439 walking** count stations. Adding non-commute utility, school, leisure, and OSM campsite/tourism layers improved baseline cycling fit from $R^2_{\log 10} = 0.352$ (commute-only) to **$0.676$** (`56.2%` within $2\times$), and walking fit from $-0.177$ to **$0.488$** (`66.8%` within $2\times$). Across the full 805.6 km spine, Phase 2 separated **route diversion** (`+3,175` bike pkm/day, `+15.4%`) from **induced/shifted commute demand** (`+4,953` bike pkm/day), while Phase 4 all-purpose modelling lifted spine cycling from `86.7` to `132.3` riders/day (`+52.6%`).
3. **Verified AMAT appraisal engine (`railactive/amat`):** A pure base-R implementation of DfT AMAT (May 2026 TAG Data Book / 2023 prices) that reproduces the official Clifton Road worked example to **£0.00** across every benefit and cost stream ($\text{BCR} = 2.840169$).

### Five Methodological Gaps to Resolve Before Scaling Up

Our audit also identified five structural weaknesses in the prototype demand pipeline that must be tightened before feeding numbers into a formal Green Book / TAG business case:

| # | Current Prototype Implementation | Economic / Appraisal Risk | Required Upgrade |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **Ad-hoc commute uplift (Phase 2 routing script):** Scenario B2 applies heuristic proximity multipliers (`+35%` on existing cyclists; up to `7.5%` car-to-bike shift) rather than a utility-based choice model. | Violates **joint modelling–valuation alignment** [@nellthorp2026, §3.1.1]: demand does not respond to the same Generalised Cost (GC) attributes valued in appraisal. | Anchor uptake in a transparent GC / logistic propensity specification with explicit corridor-exposure attenuation ($\omega_{ij}$). |
| 2 | **Unseparated leisure uplift (Phase 4 all-purpose script):** Scenario B applies hardcoded trail weights (`5.0x` vs `2.5x`) and campsite weights (`0.18` vs `0.12`) without separating route diversion from new generation. | Risks over-crediting leisure generation and obscures which trips are **Exercise & Pleasure** (marginal $VTT = 0$) vs **Other Non-Work Utility** [@nellthorp2026, §1.4.1]. | Explicitly segment outputs into TAG's four active-mode trip purposes and separate route reassignment from net trip generation. |
| 3 | **Static steady-state flows (no behavioural ramp-up lag):** `pipeline` outputs a single equilibrium daily flow; AMAT applies 100% demand in Year 1 plus a 5-year linear physiological health lag. | Overstates Present Value Benefits (PVB) by 10–25% if real-world uptake builds over 3–8 years [@goodman2014]. | Introduce an explicit behavioural adoption S-curve convolved with AMAT's physiological health lag over the 40-year ATE appraisal period. |
| 4 | **Census 2021 lockdown distortion:** Phase 2 relied on March 2021 Census OD matrices collected during COVID-19 restrictions (~31% working from home). | Distorts inter-town commuting patterns along rural corridors. | Benchmark baseline desire lines against **2011 Census OD** (pre-COVID, PCT-compatible), then apply an explicit post-COVID hybrid-working scalar. |
| 5 | **Unbridged demand-to-AMAT schema:** Link flows (`flows.parquet`) do not export OD trip lengths, `prop_on_scheme`, origin-mode diversion shares, or unpowered vs e-bike splits. | Economists cannot directly populate AMAT or ATE's forthcoming TATE3030 health tool without ad-hoc post-processing. | Define a formal 4-table hand-off schema (@sec-outputs) with built-in double-counting checks [@nellthorp2026, Table 13]. |

: Methodological audit of existing `railactive` prototype uptake scripts and required upgrades. {tbl-colwidths="[5,35,30,30]"}

## First-Principles Uptake Framework {#sec-framework}

### Joint Modelling–Valuation Alignment with Nellthorp et al. (2026)

A central principle of @nellthorp2026 (§3.1.1, p. 21) is that **demand modelling and economic valuation must be specified jointly** so that travellers' behavioural responses are driven by the exact same trip-utility attributes that enter welfare appraisal. Following Equations (6)–(10) of @nellthorp2026, the trip utility $U_r$ (and corresponding monetary Generalised Cost $GC_r = -U_r / \beta$, where $\beta$ is the marginal utility of income; @wardman2020) of an active travel route $r$ connecting origin $i$ to destination $j$ is:

$$
GC_{ij,r} = \sum_{n \in r} \Bigl( m\,v_t\,t_n + v_s\,s_n + v_e\,e_n + v_c\,c_n \Bigr) + \frac{U_{\text{pre}} + U_{\text{post}}}{\beta}
\approx \int_{0}^{T_r} \Bigl[ \beta + q(t) + e(t) \Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t + \frac{U_{\text{pre}} + U_{\text{post}}}{\beta}
$$ {#eq-gc}

where, on each link or junction $n$:

- $t_n$ is travel time (with multi-modal access/egress multiplier $m = 2.0$ where relevant);
- $s_n$ is **perceived safety threat** (fear, stress, concentration effort from motor traffic speed, volume, and HGV share — experienced in the present, and shown by @nellthorp2026 [§3.3.1] to dominate cycling deterrence, with 61% of non-cyclists citing safer roads as the key enabler in NTAS Wave 9; @dft2024ntas);
- $e_n$ is **net physical exertion** (in MET-hours, driven by distance, hilliness, and stopping/starting — which @nellthorp2026 [Eq. 14] decompose into short-term effort disutility, short-term positive exercise wellbeing, and a small perceived share $\theta \approx 0$ of discounted long-term health outcomes);
- $c_n$ is **street ambience and comfort** (surface quality, width, greenery, noise); and
- $q(t)$ bundles practical infrastructure/traffic conditions along the continuous route integral [@nellthorp2026, §3.1.6; @kouwenhoven2023].

Building a continuous, traffic-free LTN 1/20 greenway [@dft2020ltn120] along repurposed HS2 haul roads reduces perceived safety disutility $s_n$ sharply (in TAG Data Book Table A4.1.6, upgrading from "No provision" to an "Off-road segregated cycle track" is valued at **16.28 p/min** in 2023 prices; @dft2025amat), smooths gradients ($e_n$), and eliminates rural severance. That reduction $\Delta GC_{ij} < 0$ drives three distinct behavioural margins that economists must keep strictly separate:

1. **Route choice (diversion):** Existing cyclists switch from parallel hostile A/B roads onto the greenway. Net new active trips $= 0$; benefits accrue purely via **Journey Ambience** (and external safety changes) to existing users.
2. **Mode choice (mode shift):** Existing commuters switch from car driver, car passenger, bus, rail, or walking onto cycling. Generates Rule-of-a-Half user benefits ($\Delta CS$), full physical-activity health benefits (TATE3030 / AMAT), absenteeism savings, and — specifically for the **car/taxi-diverted share** — TAG Unit A5.4 Marginal External Cost (MEC) savings (decongestion, accidents, GHGs, air quality, noise, infrastructure, indirect tax).
3. **Trip generation & destination/activity choice (induced demand):** Newly generated utility or **Exercise & Pleasure** trips (crucial on a rural greenway). Generates Rule-of-a-Half user benefits (using $VTT = 0$ for Exercise & Pleasure; @nellthorp2026, §1.4.1) and full marginal health benefits, but **zero** motor-vehicle decongestion MECs.

### From Random Utility to Operational OD Propensity (PCT Logistic Curve)

Under standard Random Utility Maximisation (RUM), the probability $p_{ij}$ that a commuter on origin–destination pair $(i, j)$ chooses cycling follows a binary (or nested) logistic function of the utility difference $\Delta V_{ij} = -\lambda\,(GC^{\text{cycle}}_{ij} - GC^{\text{alt}}_{ij})$:

$$
\text{logit}\bigl(p_{ij}\bigr) = \ln\!\left(\frac{p_{ij}}{1 - p_{ij}}\right) = \alpha(q_{ij}) + f(d_{ij},\, g_{ij})
$$ {#eq-logit}

In the UK Propensity to Cycle Tool [PCT; @lovelace2017], calibrated on 2011 Census OD flows across England and Wales, the baseline distance–hilliness decay function $f(d, g)$ for fastest-route distance $d_{ij}$ (km) and average gradient $g_{ij}$ (%) is:

$$
\text{logit}\bigl(p^{\text{base}}_{ij}\bigr) = -3.818 - 0.652\,d_{ij} + 2.084\sqrt{d_{ij}} + 0.00878\,d_{ij}^2 - 0.256\,g_{ij} + 0.0199\,d_{ij}g_{ij} - 0.123\sqrt{d_{ij}}\,g_{ij}
$$ {#eq-pct-base}

Because $d_{ij}$ and $g_{ij}$ are observed directly for every 2011 LSOA pair, an area-wide transformation to Dutch-standard infrastructure (*Go Dutch*) acts primarily as a parallel shift in the infrastructure-quality intercept ($\Delta \alpha_{\text{Dutch}} = +2.552$, with a slight distance slope adjustment $-0.079\,d_{ij}$), while *E-bikes* additionally attenuates the distance and gradient penalties $e(t)$ — directly reflecting the reduced MET-hour effort disutility of electrically assisted cycles [@nellthorp2026, §4.2.3].

### Scheme-Exposure Attenuation ($\omega_{ij}$): Avoiding Single-Corridor Over-Attribution

A common error in active travel appraisals is crediting 100% of an **area-wide** *Go Dutch* network scenario to a **single linear corridor**. An OD desire line crossing perpendicular to the greenway — or starting 2.5 km away from an access point — receives only a fraction of the $\Delta GC$ experienced by a trip whose origin, destination, and route lie directly on the spine.

From first principles, we therefore define a transparent, dimensionless **corridor exposure weight** $\omega_{ij} \in [0, 1]$ for each OD pair:

$$
\omega_{ij} = \phi_{ij} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{a_i + a_j}{L_a}\right)
$$ {#eq-omega}

where $\phi_{ij} \in [0, 1]$ is the fraction of the straight-line desire line falling within a 1.5 km lateral corridor buffer, $a_i$ and $a_j$ are the Euclidean access/egress distances (m) from the origin and destination population-weighted centroids to the greenway spine, and $L_a = 3{,}000\text{ m}$ is the combined access-decay scale (meaning an OD pair with $a_i = a_j = 500\text{ m}$ and $\phi_{ij} = 1$ retains $\omega_{ij} = e^{-1/3} = 0.72$, whereas a pair 2.5 km from the spine at both ends retains only $e^{-5/3} = 0.19$).

For any corridor investment scenario achieving a fraction $\kappa \in (0, 1]$ of the Dutch-quality infrastructure gap along the scheme itself, predicted steady-state commute cyclists $C^{1}_{ij}$ are:

$$
C^{1}_{ij} = \min\!\Bigl(N_{ij},\; C^{0}_{ij} + \kappa\,\omega_{ij}\,\max\bigl(0,\; C^{\text{ref}}_{ij} - C^{0}_{ij}\bigr)\Bigr)
$$ {#eq-corridor-uptake}

where $N_{ij}$ is total commuters, $C^{0}_{ij}$ is observed baseline cyclists, and $C^{\text{ref}}_{ij}$ is the PCT *Go Dutch* (Central, $\kappa = 0.50$) or *E-bikes* (High, $\kappa = 0.60$) upper-envelope benchmark. This keeps the model **strictly bounded**, **monotone in access proximity and alignment**, and **immediately auditable** by economists.

## Case Study: Oxfordshire to Uxbridge (`r tot_len_km` km) {#sec-casestudy}

### Corridor Geography and Infrastructure Profile

To demonstrate the framework on a tractable, diverse, and policy-relevant stretch before full-corridor roll-out, we select the **`r tot_len_km` km Oxfordshire-to-Uxbridge section** of the preferred North–South Greenway (v0.5.2, Sections `13, 10, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 12, 11`, comprising `r nrow(corr)` preferred links). Running south-east from **Banbury** (Cherwell District, Oxfordshire) via **Brackley**, **Finmere/Mixbury** (northern Oxfordshire), **Calvert/Quainton**, **Aylesbury**, **Wendover**, **Great Missenden**, **Amersham**, and the **Colne Valley** into **Uxbridge** (London Borough of Hillingdon), this section spans rural market towns, HS2 civil engineering haul roads, Chiltern valleys, and outer-London commuter catchments.

```{r tbl-infra}
class_disp <- class_sum |>
  mutate(
    `Corridor Classification` = classification,
    `Links` = n_links,
    `Length (km)` = sprintf("%.2f", length_km),
    `Share (%)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", share_pct)
  ) |>
  select(`Corridor Classification`, `Links`, `Length (km)`, `Share (%)`)

kable(
  class_disp,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Preferred Oxfordshire–Uxbridge corridor breakdown by infrastructure classification (v0.5.2, Sections 13 to 11)."
)
```

Over **64% (`72.0 km`)** of the corridor comprises off-road or segregated active travel assets — led by **Repurposed HS2 Temporary Construction Roads (`21.7 km`, `19.3%`)**, **Upgraded PRoW (`19.5 km`)**, **New Greenway (`19.3 km`)**, **Canal Towpath Upgrades (`7.2 km`)**, and **Main Road Cycle Tracks (`4.0 km`)** — linked by quietways (`18.6 km`), existing routes (`13.4 km`), and quiet lanes (`8.4 km`).

### 2011 OD Commute Uptake Potential Across the Corridor

Extracting all inter-LSOA 2011 Census commute desire lines ($\le 20\text{ km}$ fastest-route distance) whose origin and destination centroids lie within 3 km of the Oxfordshire–Uxbridge spine yields **`r comma(n_pairs_3km)` OD pairs** representing **`r comma(tot_comm_3km)` daily commuters** (`59.1%` car drivers, `25.0%` walking, and only **`3.92%` (`r comma(base_cyc_3km)`)** cycling). Restricting to the **core corridor-aligned subset** (both endpoints $\le 1.5\text{ km}$ from the spine, $\ge 70\%$ of the desire line within 1.5 km, distance $1.5\text{–}20\text{ km}$) isolates **`r comma(n_pairs_core)` OD pairs** and **`r comma(tot_comm_core)` commuters** (`4.29%` baseline cycling) whose journeys directly align with the proposed greenway.

```{r tbl-scenarios}
scen_tbl <- tibble(
  Scenario = c(
    "Baseline (2011 Census Observed)",
    "PCT Government Target (National Benchmark)",
    "Corridor Central (50% Go Dutch, attenuated)",
    "Corridor High (60% E-bikes, attenuated)",
    "PCT Go Dutch (Unattenuated Area Ceiling)",
    "PCT E-bikes (Unattenuated Area Ceiling)"
  ),
  `3 km Cyclists` = round(c(base_cyc_3km, gt_cyc_3km, cc_cyc_3km, ch_cyc_3km, du_cyc_3km, eb_cyc_3km)),
  `3 km New` = round(c(0, gt_cyc_3km - base_cyc_3km, cc_cyc_3km - base_cyc_3km,
                       ch_cyc_3km - base_cyc_3km, du_cyc_3km - base_cyc_3km, eb_cyc_3km - base_cyc_3km)),
  `3 km Share` = percent(c(base_cyc_3km, gt_cyc_3km, cc_cyc_3km, ch_cyc_3km, du_cyc_3km, eb_cyc_3km) / tot_comm_3km, accuracy = 0.1),
  `Core Aligned Cyclists` = round(c(
    base_cyc_core,
    sum(core$govtarget_slc),
    cc_cyc_core,
    ch_cyc_core,
    du_cyc_core,
    eb_cyc_core
  )),
  `Core New` = round(c(
    0,
    sum(core$govtarget_slc) - base_cyc_core,
    cc_cyc_core - base_cyc_core,
    ch_cyc_core - base_cyc_core,
    du_cyc_core - base_cyc_core,
    eb_cyc_core - base_cyc_core
  )),
  `Core Share` = percent(c(
    base_cyc_core, sum(core$govtarget_slc), cc_cyc_core, ch_cyc_core, du_cyc_core, eb_cyc_core
  ) / tot_comm_core, accuracy = 0.1)
) |>
  mutate(across(c(`3 km Cyclists`, `3 km New`, `Core Aligned Cyclists`, `Core New`), comma))

kable(
  scen_tbl,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Estimated steady-state commute cycling uptake along the Oxfordshire–Uxbridge corridor (2011 Census OD baseline, inter-LSOA pairs <= 20 km)."
)
```

Three findings stand out immediately for economic appraisal:

1. **Corridor-exposure attenuation matters enormously:** Unattenuated *Go Dutch* yields `+16,336` commute cyclists across the 3 km catchment, but once we attenuate by scheme alignment and access distance ($\omega_{ij}$) with $\kappa = 0.50$, the **Corridor Central** estimate is **`+4,096` new commute cyclists** (`11.6%` mode share), of whom **`+2,454` (`60%`)** sit in the tightly aligned core subset (`14.9%` mode share).
2. **Spatial concentration around key nodal hubs:** Demand clusters strongly around **Aylesbury**, **Banbury**, **Uxbridge/Denham**, and **Amersham/Chalfonts** (@fig-dist-lad). Rural inter-village links (Sections 4–7 around Calvert, Steeple Claydon, and Finmere) carry much lower commute volume and will rely far more heavily on **leisure/tourism** and **e-bike** demand.
3. **Distance profile and the e-bike unlock:** Conventional cycling uptake peaks sharply at `2–6 km`, whereas **e-bikes** disproportionately unlock the **`6–15 km` inter-settlement band** (such as Wendover–Aylesbury, King's Sutton–Banbury, and Chalfont St Peter–Uxbridge) where rural greenway segments sit.

## Worked Example Desire Line: Commuting, Leisure Extension & Temporal Lag {#sec-worked-example}

### Step-by-Step Commute Calculation: King's Sutton to Banbury

To make the mechanics completely transparent for economists, we trace a single real 2011 Census OD desire line at the Oxfordshire end of the corridor: **`E01027288 -> E01028435` (King's Sutton, South Northamptonshire border $\rightarrow$ Banbury Town Centre, Cherwell / Oxfordshire)**.

- **Observed 2011 attributes:** $N_{ij} = 55$ daily commuters: **`0` cyclists**, `1` walker, **`34` car drivers (`61.8%`)**, `8` car passengers, `7` bus, and `5` rail. Fastest road distance $d_{ij} = 7.84\text{ km}$, average slope $g_{ij} = 1.50\%$.
- **Corridor alignment:** Origin centroid is `246 m` from the preferred greenway spine (Section 10/13); destination centroid in central Banbury is `400 m` from the spine; **100%** of the straight-line desire line lies within 1 km of the greenway ($\phi_{ij} = 1.00$).

**Step 1 — Baseline & upper-envelope logistic propensities (@eq-pct-base):**
Evaluating the PCT logistic curve at $d = 7.84\text{ km}$ and $g = 1.50\%$ gives a UK baseline propensity of $p^{\text{base}} = 3.82\%$ (`2.10` cyclists under *Government Target*), a *Go Dutch* propensity of $p^{\text{Dutch}} = 21.29\%$ (`11.71` cyclists), and an *E-bikes* propensity of $p^{\text{ebike}} = 31.82\%$ (`17.50` cyclists). Observed baseline cycling is `0`, reflecting severe traffic-stress deterrence ($s_0$) on existing rural roads into Banbury.

**Step 2 — Corridor exposure weight (@eq-omega) and steady-state commute uptake (@eq-corridor-uptake):**
$$
\omega_{ij} = 1.00 \times \exp\!\left(-\frac{246 + 400}{3{,}000}\right) = 0.8064
$$
Under **Corridor Central** ($\kappa = 0.50$ of the *Go Dutch* gap), steady-state commute cyclists rise from **`0` to `4.72` commuters** (`+4.72` new cyclists; `8.6%` mode share). Applying the standard AMAT return-trip factor ($1 + 0.90 = 1.90$) and `220` commuting days/year yields **`8.97` one-way cycle trips/day** (`1,973` trips/year, **`15,471` cycle-km/year** on this single LSOA pair). Under **Corridor High (E-bikes, $\kappa = 0.60$)**, uptake rises to **`8.47` commute cyclists** (`16.09` daily one-way trips).

**Step 3 — Mode diversion decomposition (for TAG Unit A5.4 MECs):**
Under proportional diversion from non-cycling modes (PCT default), `34 / 55 = 61.8%` of new cyclists (`2.92` commuters) divert from **car driver**, `14.5%` from car passenger, `21.8%` from public transport, and `1.8%` from walking. However, AMAT's national default car-driver diversion rate is only `24%` (plus `6%` taxi; @dft2025amat). On a car-dominated rural corridor like King's Sutton–Banbury (`62%` car driver), using the national urban default understates displaced vehicle-km by more than half — illustrating why **OD-specific diversion shares** (Option 3 in @sec-questions) should be passed into economic appraisal.

### Extending the Model to Leisure and Exercise/Pleasure Trips

Commuting accounts for only **29.9%** of cycling trips in the National Travel Survey (2022–2024) and **29.5%** of cycling minutes in the Active Lives Survey (Year 9), whereas **leisure cycling accounts for 39.7% of trips and 70.5% of total cycling time** (with longer mean trip distances of `6.76 km` vs `5.52 km` for commuting; see [Methodology](methods.qmd)). On rural greenway sections like Banbury–Brackley–Calvert, omitting leisure understates total demand by a factor of **3 to 5**.

Crucially, @nellthorp2026 (§1.4.1, Table 2, p. 4) demonstrate that active mode appraisal requires **four trip purposes**, splitting out **Exercise & Pleasure** (where utility resides in the journey itself: leisure rides, dog walking, running) from **Other Non-Work Utility** (shopping, education, visiting friends, station access):

- For **Exercise & Pleasure** trips (estimated at ~30% of all main-mode active trips nationally, and substantially higher on traffic-free rural greenways), **marginal Value of Travel Time ($VTT$) equals zero**: shortening a recreational ride leads users to ride further rather than bank time savings [@nellthorp2026, p. x, fn 79].
- However, Exercise & Pleasure trips **still generate full Journey Ambience / perceived safety user benefits** (via Rule of a Half) and **full physical-activity health benefits** (mortality and morbidity via AMAT / TATE3030), though with **lower car-diversion MECs** because many are newly generated or displaced from alternative leisure activities rather than car commutes.

In operational modelling, the commute desire-line framework extends to leisure in two transparent tiers:

1. **Tier 1 — Empirical purpose expansion (rapid screening / sensitivity):** Scale commute uptake on each corridor segment using purpose ratios calibrated to NTS/ALS and rural greenway counter evidence (in Phase 4 of `railactive/pipeline`, HS2 Alignment links average `21.9` daily commute cyclists vs `16.4` local leisure + `27.2` tourism/day-trip + `15.1` education/utility = `80.6` total daily cyclists, a **3.7× all-purpose multiplier** on commuting). Applied to the King's Sutton–Banbury desire line (`8.97` daily commute trips under Corridor Central), a conservative `1.5×` local leisure + `0.5×` other-utility ratio adds **`+13.5` leisure/exercise trips/day** and **`+4.5` other-utility trips/day** (`27.0` total daily trips), tagged explicitly with `purpose = exercise_pleasure` ($VTT = 0$, lower car diversion) vs `purpose = other_utility`.
2. **Tier 2 — Dedicated spatial leisure/tourism gravity model (full-scale corridor):** Generate explicit OD flows from residential zones (LSOAs/OAs), rail stations, and OSM campsites/stays to greenway trail points, country parks, and heritage attractors (as prototyped in `pipeline` Phase 4), using a **longer distance-decay parameter** ($L \approx 6\text{–}9\text{ km}$ vs $3\text{–}5\text{ km}$ for utility) and an explicit loop-ride / out-and-back factor, calibrated directly against weekend vs weekday counter ratios at rural trail counters.

### Modelling Change Over Time Including Behavioural and Physiological Lags

@nellthorp2026 (§2.3, fn 28 & 30) note that ATE uses a **40-year appraisal period** for active travel infrastructure (compared with 60 years in TAG Unit A1.1), discounting transport benefits at **3.5%** and health benefits at **1.5% (1.29% long-term)** from a 2023 base year [@hmt2026greenbook]. While AMAT incorporates a 5-year linear **physiological health lag** ($h_k = \min(1, 0.2k)$ for years $k = 1\dots 5$ after an individual becomes active), **neither AMAT nor @nellthorp2026 currently specifies a behavioural demand ramp-up lag**. Longitudinal evaluations of new UK traffic-free routes (e.g. the iConnect study; @goodman2014) show that behaviour adjusts gradually over 2–5+ years as awareness spreads, habits shift, and bikes/e-bikes are acquired.

To capture both mechanisms transparently, let $r(t) \in [0, 1]$ denote the cumulative **behavioural adoption share** at time $t$ years post-opening, modelled via a **Bass diffusion S-curve** [@bass1969] with innovation parameter $p$ (early adopters responding immediately on opening) and imitation/network-effect parameter $q$:

$$
r(t) = \frac{1 - e^{-(p + q)t}}{1 + \frac{q}{p}\,e^{-(p + q)t}}
$$ {#eq-bass}

In appraisal year $y \ge oy$ (with $t_y = y - oy + 0.5$ at mid-year), new daily trips equal:

$$
\Delta T_y = \Delta T^{*} \cdot r(t_y) \cdot (1 + g_{\text{bg}})^{\min(y - oy,\, 20)}
$$ {#eq-annual-trips}

where $\Delta T^{*}$ is steady-state equilibrium uptake and $g_{\text{bg}} = 0.0075$ is AMAT's annual background user growth rate. Because each annual cohort of newly converted riders $\Delta r_j = r(t_j) - r(t_{j-1})$ enters at year $j$ and then builds physiological mortality protection over 5 years, the **effective health-benefit share** $H^{\text{eff}}_k$ in operational year $k$ is the exact discrete convolution:

$$
H^{\text{eff}}_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \Delta r_j \cdot \min\!\bigl(1,\; 0.2\,(k - j + 1)\bigr)
$$ {#eq-conv}

```{r fig-lag}
#| fig-cap: "Temporal trajectory over ATE's 40-year appraisal period (2030–2069) on the King's Sutton–Banbury worked example (Corridor Central): (A) annual commute cycling trips under instant jump vs Fast (3-yr), Central (5-yr), and Slow (8-yr) Bass ramp-up; (B) effective health-benefit share after convolving behavioural adoption with AMAT's 5-year physiological lag."
#| fig-width: 10.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
#| dpi: 300

yrs <- 0:39
cal_yr <- 2030 + yrs
t_mid <- yrs + 0.5
grow <- (1.0075) ^ pmin(yrs, 20)
disc_t <- 1 / (1.035 ^ yrs)
disc_h <- 1 / (1.015 ^ yrs)
h_lag_std <- pmin(1.0, (yrs + 1) * 0.2)

bass <- function(t, p, q) (1 - exp(-(p + q) * t)) / (1 + (q / p) * exp(-(p + q) * t))

# Calibrated profiles: Fast (~80% by yr 3), Central (~78% by yr 5), Slow (~79% by yr 8)
profiles <- list(
  "Instant (AMAT Default)" = rep(1.0, 40),
  "Fast Ramp-Up (3-yr)"    = bass(t_mid, p = 0.22, q = 0.70),
  "Central Ramp-Up (5-yr)" = bass(t_mid, p = 0.10, q = 0.55),
  "Slow Ramp-Up (8-yr)"    = bass(t_mid, p = 0.05, q = 0.35)
)

convolve_health <- function(r) {
  dr <- c(r[1], diff(r))
  he <- numeric(length(r))
  for (k in seq_along(r)) {
    for (j in seq_len(k)) {
      he[k] <- he[k] + dr[j] * min(1.0, (k - j + 1) * 0.2)
    }
  }
  he
}

ex_eq_annual_trips <- ex_main$corr_central_slc * 1.9 * 220 # ~1,973 trips/yr

lag_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(profiles), function(nm) {
  r <- profiles[[nm]]
  he <- convolve_health(r)
  tibble(
    Year = cal_yr,
    Profile = nm,
    Annual_Trips = ex_eq_annual_trips * r * grow,
    Health_Eff = he
  )
})) |>
  mutate(Profile = factor(Profile, levels = names(profiles)))

lag_pal <- c(
  "Instant (AMAT Default)" = "#64748b",
  "Fast Ramp-Up (3-yr)"    = "#0284c7",
  "Central Ramp-Up (5-yr)" = "#1e3a8a",
  "Slow Ramp-Up (8-yr)"    = "#d97706"
)

p_lag1 <- ggplot(lag_df |> filter(Year <= 2050), aes(x = Year, y = Annual_Trips, colour = Profile, linetype = Profile)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = lag_pal, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid", "solid", "solid"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "A. Annual Commute Trips (King's Sutton -> Banbury)", x = "Appraisal year (first 20 yrs shown)", y = "One-way commute cycle trips / yr") +
  theme_rail(9.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))

p_lag2 <- ggplot(lag_df |> filter(Year <= 2045), aes(x = Year, y = Health_Eff, colour = Profile, linetype = Profile)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = lag_pal, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid", "solid", "solid"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "B. Effective Health Share (Behavioural + 5-Yr Health Lag)", x = "Appraisal year (first 15 yrs shown)", y = "Share of steady-state health effect") +
  theme_rail(9.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))

p_lag1 + p_lag2
```

```{r tbl-lag-pv}
lag_pv_raw <- bind_rows(lapply(names(profiles), function(nm) {
  r <- profiles[[nm]]
  he <- convolve_health(r)
  pv_t <- sum(r * grow * disc_t) / sum(profiles[[1]] * grow * disc_t)
  pv_h <- sum(he * grow * disc_h) / sum(h_lag_std * grow * disc_h)
  tibble(
    Profile = nm,
    Yr1 = r[1], Yr3 = r[3], Yr5 = r[5],
    pv_t = pv_t, pv_h = pv_h
  )
}))

pv_t_central <- lag_pv_raw$pv_t[lag_pv_raw$Profile == "Central Ramp-Up (5-yr)"]
pv_h_central <- lag_pv_raw$pv_h[lag_pv_raw$Profile == "Central Ramp-Up (5-yr)"]

# Verified railactive/amat instant-jump PVB components (£m, 2023 prices, 40-yr 2030-2069) for Core Aligned Commute
amat_health_inst <- 48.497
amat_amb_inst    <- 39.673
amat_abs_inst    <- 8.648
amat_mec_inst    <- 5.429 + 0.564 + 0.320 + 0.145 + 0.036 + 0.025
amat_tot_inst    <- amat_health_inst + amat_amb_inst + amat_abs_inst + amat_mec_inst

amat_health_lag  <- amat_health_inst * pv_h_central
amat_amb_lag     <- amat_amb_inst * pv_t_central
amat_abs_lag     <- amat_abs_inst * pv_t_central
amat_mec_lag     <- amat_mec_inst * pv_t_central
amat_tot_lag     <- amat_health_lag + amat_amb_lag + amat_abs_lag + amat_mec_lag

lag_pv_tbl <- lag_pv_raw |>
  transmute(
    `Adoption Profile` = Profile,
    `Yr 1 Share` = percent(Yr1, accuracy = 1),
    `Yr 3 Share` = percent(Yr3, accuracy = 1),
    `Yr 5 Share` = percent(Yr5, accuracy = 1),
    `40-Yr Transport PV Factor (3.5%)` = sprintf("%.3f (%+.1f%%)", pv_t, 100 * (pv_t - 1)),
    `40-Yr Health PV Factor (1.5%)` = sprintf("%.3f (%+.1f%%)", pv_h, 100 * (pv_h - 1))
  )

kable(
  lag_pv_tbl,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Impact of behavioural adoption ramp-up on 40-year Present Value benefits (2030–2069) relative to AMAT's instant-jump default."
)
```

Notice the key economic insight in @tbl-lag-pv: under a realistic **5-year Central ramp-up**, 40-year **transport/ambience PV falls by `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - pv_t_central))`**, whereas **health PV falls by `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - pv_h_central))`** — a smaller percentage drop despite the compounded physiological lag, because Green Book health discounting (`1.5%`) weights later years much more heavily than transport discounting (`3.5%`).

## Output Datasets for the Economic Evaluation Side {#sec-outputs}

To create a clean, auditable contract between the spatial demand team and the consultancy's economic appraisal models (`railactive/amat`, TAG worksheets, and ATE's forthcoming **TATE3030** morbidity/mortality tool), the uptake pipeline will output **four standardised tables**:

| Output Dataset | Granularity | Key Fields & Units | Economic Appraisal Consumer |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. OD Uptake** (`od_uptake.parquet`) | OD pair $\times$ Purpose (`commute`, `business`, `other_utility`, `exercise_pleasure`) $\times$ Mode (`walk`, `cycle`, `ebike`) $\times$ Scenario | `o_id`, `d_id`, `section_id`, `rf_dist_km`, `slope_pct`, `omega_corr`, `prop_on_scheme`, `trips_base`, `trips_with`, `trips_new`, `divert_car`, `divert_pt`, `divert_walk`, `induced_share`, `delta_met_wk` | TAG Unit A5.4 MECs (car-km displaced), TATE3030 health MET-hours, Rule-of-a-Half $\Delta CS$ |
| **2. Link Flows** (`link_flows.parquet`) | Network link $\times$ Section $\times$ Scenario | `link_id`, `gw_id`, `section`, `class`, `length_km`, `infra_base`, `infra_prop`, `flow_base`, `flow_diverted`, `flow_induced`, `pkm_base`, `pkm_with`, `grade_pct`, `lts_base`, `lts_prop` | Link-level Journey Ambience ($\Delta\text{Rate} \times \text{Time on Scheme}$), Safety exposure & external casualty costs, scheme prioritisation |
| **3. Annual Profile** (`annual_demand.csv`) | Section $\times$ Year ($2030\dots 2069$) $\times$ Purpose $\times$ Mode | `section`, `year`, `ramp_share`, `health_eff`, `trips_exist_yr`, `trips_new_yr`, `vkm_saved_yr`, `met_hrs_yr` | 40-year discounted PVB stream (3.5% transport / 1.5% health) with explicit ramp-up & background growth |
| **4. AMAT Inputs** (`amat_inputs.csv`) | Corridor Section (or Route Case) $\times$ Scenario | Direct arguments for `amat::amat_run()`: `cycle_trips_without`, `cycle_trips_with`, `cycle_trip_km`, `cycle_prop_on_scheme`, `cycle_current_infra`, `cycle_proposed_infra`, `annual_days`, `car_divert`, `prop_employed`, plus `ramp_pv_t` & `ramp_pv_h` | Automated batch appraisal via `railactive/amat` (zero manual spreadsheet entry) |

: Standardised output contract between the RailActive demand pipeline and economic evaluation tools. {tbl-colwidths="[22,22,32,24]"}

### Illustrative Economic Scale (Core Aligned Commute Subset Only)

Passing just the **core corridor-aligned commuting subset** (`r comma(n_pairs_core)` OD pairs, `+2,454` new commute cyclists = `+4,663` daily one-way trips, mean new trip distance **`r sprintf("%.2f", mean_dist_core_new)` km**, `prop_on_scheme = 0.72`, `220` commuting days/year, `2030–2069` 40-year appraisal period, AMAT default `24%` car diversion) through `railactive/amat` yields an **instant-jump PVB of £`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_tot_inst)`m** (2023 prices, discounted to 2023) — or **£`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_tot_lag)`m** (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (amat_tot_lag / amat_tot_inst - 1))`) after applying our **Central 5-year behavioural ramp-up**:

- **Health (Premature Death):** £`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_health_inst)`m instant $\rightarrow$ **£`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_health_lag)`m** with 5-year ramp-up (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * amat_health_lag / amat_tot_lag)` of PVB)
- **Journey Ambience:** £`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_amb_inst)`m instant $\rightarrow$ **£`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_amb_lag)`m** with 5-year ramp-up (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * amat_amb_lag / amat_tot_lag)` of PVB)
- **Workplace Absenteeism:** £`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_abs_inst)`m instant $\rightarrow$ **£`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_abs_lag)`m** with 5-year ramp-up (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * amat_abs_lag / amat_tot_lag)` of PVB)
- **Decongestion & Environmental MECs** (Congestion £5.4m, Accidents £0.56m, GHGs £0.32m, Indirect Tax £0.15m, Noise/AQ £0.06m): £`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_mec_inst)`m instant $\rightarrow$ **£`r sprintf("%.1f", amat_mec_lag)`m** with 5-year ramp-up (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * amat_mec_lag / amat_tot_lag)` of PVB)

Crucially, **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (amat_health_lag + amat_amb_lag) / amat_tot_lag)` of total commuting PVB sits in Health and Journey Ambience** — before adding **morbidity** (TATE3030), **walking**, **education/utility**, or **leisure/tourism** demand. That concentration makes adherence to @nellthorp2026's double-counting rules essential:

::: {.callout-important}
### Double-Counting Compliance Checklist

Following Table 13 (Recommendations 1–10) of @nellthorp2026:

1. **User benefits vs long-term health (Recs 1–2):** Retain $\theta \approx 0$ as the working assumption — Journey Ambience user benefits and AMAT/TATE3030 long-term health benefits are **additive** (do not deduct perceived health from TATE3030 unless future DCE evidence establishes $\theta > 0$, in which case deduct $\theta \times$ *internal* health benefits only).
2. **Rule of a Half boundary (§2.4, fn 58):** Apply RoH *only* to Consumer Surplus / Journey Ambience ($\Delta CS$); do **not** halve physical-activity health benefits or mode-shift MECs.
3. **User benefits vs safety (Recs 3–6):** Because AMAT Journey Ambience (`16.28 p/min` for off-road segregated track) already embeds users' own perceived safety WTP — which is 2–4× objective own casualty-reduction WTP — **never add TAG own-casualty WTP on top**. Add only *external* safety outcome costs (NHS, net output, police, insurance admin, injuries to others) plus mode-shift safety MECs.
4. **Place quality / urban realm (Recs 7–10):** Only value destination/origin place quality ($p_i, p_j$) for dwell time or short movements strictly **outside** the trips already captured by the transport model.
5. **Exercise & Pleasure VTT (§1.4.1):** Set marginal $VTT = 0$ for Exercise & Pleasure trips, while retaining their Journey Ambience and TATE3030 health benefits.
:::

## Options and Questions Before Scaling to the Full Corridor {#sec-questions}

Before scaling this workflow from Oxfordshire–Uxbridge (`112.5 km`) to the entire **805.6 km North–South Greenway**, we recommend agreeing the following eight methodological decisions with the consultancy economics team and John Nellthorp:

| # | Decision Area | Options to Consider | Recommended Default & Rationale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **Commute baseline year & WFH adjustment** | (a) 2011 Census OD unadjusted; (b) 2021 Census OD; (c) **2011 Census OD spatial pattern scaled to 2026 employment & post-COVID commuting days/wk** (e.g., NTS 2023–24 `~3.8` office days/wk vs `4.6` in 2011). | **Option (c):** Avoids March 2021 lockdown distortion while transparently reflecting hybrid working via `annual_days` (e.g., 190–200 days/yr vs 220). |
| 2 | **Uptake model engine at scale** | (a) Attenuated PCT OD framework ($\kappa, \omega_{ij}$, fast & auditable); (b) Full GC-elasticity discrete-choice model coupled to `netassign` shortest-path $\Delta GC_{ij}$; (c) **Hybrid:** `netassign` computes link-level $\Delta GC_{ij}$ and `prop_on_scheme`, driving a unified logit uptake equation. | **Option (c)** for full business case (achieves full joint alignment with @nellthorp2026 §3.1.1); **Option (a)** as transparent sensitivity benchmark. |
| 3 | **Car-diversion share (MECs)** | (a) National AMAT default (`24%` car + `6%` taxi); (b) **OD-specific proportional diversion** from 2011/2021 non-cycling mode shares; (c) Nested logit separating `{Walk, Cycle}` from `{Car, PT}`. | **Report (a) as TAG Core and (b)/(c) as Sensitivity:** On rural corridors (`59–62%` car share), AMAT's urban default materially understates displaced car-km. |
| 4 | **Leisure & tourism demand methodology** | (a) Empirical NTS/ALS purpose multipliers; (b) **Dedicated spatial gravity model** (residents + stations + OSM campsites $\rightarrow$ greenway/heritage attractors) calibrated to rural trail counters; (c) ORVal recreation demand integration. | **Option (b)** with explicit split between *Other Non-Work Utility* and *Exercise & Pleasure* ($VTT = 0$, lower car diversion), cross-checked against (a). |
| 5 | **Behavioural ramp-up lag** | (a) AMAT default (instant 100% Year 1); (b) Linear 3–5 yr build-up; (c) **Bass S-curve (Central 5-yr maturity)** convolved with AMAT's 5-yr physiological health lag, with 3-yr/8-yr sensitivities. | **Option (c):** Realistic, empirically grounded [@goodman2014], and guards against BCR optimism bias in Green Book assurance. |
| 6 | **E-bike segmentation** | (a) Pool all cycling as unpowered; (b) **Explicit unpowered vs e-bike split** (different distance/slope elasticity, lower MET intensity ~`4.5–5.0` vs `6.8` METs, higher average speed ~`18–20 km/h`). | **Option (b):** Explicitly recommended by @nellthorp2026 (§4.2.3) and decisive for `6–15 km` rural inter-town links. |
| 7 | **Appraisal period & TATE3030 transition** | (a) Standard AMAT 20-year period; (b) **ATE 40-year infrastructure period** (matching @nellthorp2026 fn 28); (c) TAG A1.1 60-year period. Also confirm timing for incorporating ATE's TATE3030 morbidity tool alongside AMAT mortality. | **Option (b) (40 years)** as core with 20-year AMAT sensitivity; structure outputs (`delta_met_wk` by demographic segment) to be TATE3030-ready. |
| 8 | **Spatial aggregation & boundary double-counting** | (a) Whole-corridor unified appraisal; (b) **Modular Route Cases / Section appraisals** (e.g., Oxfordshire–Uxbridge, Calvert–Quainton, Warwickshire) with cross-boundary trips allocated proportionally by `prop_on_scheme`. | **Option (b) summing cleanly to (a):** Allows phasing/funding prioritisation across local authorities without double-counting cross-section trips. |

: Key methodological options and decision register before full-corridor roll-out. {tbl-colwidths="[5,22,41,32]"}
